messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Maria had been twelve years into her vocation when the night her brother, an infantry officer in Afghanistan, was taken down by a roadside bomb turned into the flashpoint of her life. They had been walking home from a brief respite in the forward operating base, the sky a bruised orange as artillery hissed in the distance. The explosion came from behind, a sudden burst of metal that cracked the air, and Maria saw her brother collapse, his fingers slackening as the world went black. In the seconds that followed, she pressed herself against the broken concrete, a hand trembling, trying to grasp something, anything, to stop the blood from splattering onto the earth. She could not see the fatal bullet, only the blur of his face, the flash of white as he went still. It was that instant of partial clarity, the part of the memory that felt like a knife, that would later haunt her every waking moment. She had come to believe that if she had been quicker, if she had moved with a different instinct, he might have survived. The guilt gnawed at her, a relentless reminder that she was not a shield for those she loved. This self-blame was the first crack in the edifice of her faith, the voice that said, “I failed to protect.” From that moment she began to distance herself from everything that had touched that night. The abandoned road, the stretch of dirt that had become a marker of loss, became a place she would no longer cross. She would stare at the photograph of her brother and mentally recite prayers, a ritual she had invented, hoping the words could bind the violence away. She even went so far as to refuse to sit in the pews where her mother’s ashes were placed, fearing that the scent of lilies would stir the memory. These avoidance moves—steering clear of the site, performing mental rituals, shunning reminders—were all born of her feeling that she could no longer rely on herself to keep safe. The first time a mundane scent triggered her was on a Wednesday morning, when a neighbor’s car alarm wailed while Maria was preparing the convent’s communal breakfast. The sharp, metallic tang of the alarm lifted the memory of the explosive burst, and the scene unfolded in vivid detail: the crunch of debris, the brother’s last gasp, the white of his eyes. She could not control the sudden surge; the memory burst through without warning, unbidden and complete. That instant magnified her sense of failure, as if the intruding image was a verdict that she still had not been able to protect. Her mind clung to the image, and the more she avoided the triggers, the more her brain kept the memory alive, as if every missed opportunity to confront the past sharpened its edges. Her avoidance habits grew more entrenched. She began to notice the slightest hint of danger in the mundane: the smell of antiseptic in the convent’s infirmary, the murmur of a radio report about an upcoming battle. Each cue sent her spiraling back to that night, reinforcing the idea that she could never again trust her own judgment. She would stand on the periphery of her own life, watching the others who walked in with open faces, believing that her internal rituals could not keep the world safe. The mental loops she spun—repeating prayers, visualizing shields—only served to strengthen her conviction that she was the cause of her brother’s death. Every avoidance she practiced fed back into the memory, deepening the recall, and every time the memory surfaced she grew more convinced that she had failed. The cycle tightened; the more she tried to keep the past at bay, the more she felt powerless, and the more she leaned into those rituals, hoping that her faith could reverse what her own hands could not. Today, Maria sits in a small cloistered chapel, the quiet too loud for her. The church’s stained glass no longer offers her comfort; instead, the colors seem to flicker with the flashes of a battlefield. She no longer participates in the weekly sermon because the words sound like a prelude to the bomb. The distance she keeps from her own memories has carved a chasm between her and her fellow sisters, leaving her work—her singing of hymns, her tending of the garden—feeling hollow. She has been coming to the parish office more often, seeking solace in conversation, but her mind keeps circling back to the night that has become her anchor. The only change that has pierced the gloom is the realization that she cannot continue to live in a world where she cannot rely on herself, where her thoughts and rituals keep her isolated. Her hope is simple: to find a way to walk back through the memories without the weight of self-blame that holds her in place, to regain trust in her own ability to protect the fragile life she now holds within her convent walls.
